 1   INTRODUCTION
 2   Q.   Please state your name, occupation and business address.

 3   A.   My name is Daren K. Zigich. I am a Licensed Professional Engineer employed by the New

 4        Mexico Public Regulation Commission (“NMPRC” or “Commission”) in the Utility

 5        Division. My business address is P.O. Box 1269, Santa Fe, NM 87504.

 6

 7   Q.   Please summarize your educational background.

 8   A.   I have a Bachelor of Aerospace Engineering and Mechanics from the University of

 9        Minnesota, in Minneapolis, MN and a Master of Science in Mechanical Engineering from

10        New Mexico State University, in Las Cruces, NM. I am also a Licensed Professional

11        Engineer in New Mexico, Minnesota, Idaho, and California, and have for nearly 30 years

12        maintained or exceeded the professional development (continuing education) requirements

13        of each licensing jurisdiction.

14

15   Q.   Please summarize your professional experience.

16   A.   In my over 36 year career, I have had the pleasure to work in both the public and private

17        sectors spanning disciplines such as being a guidance, navigation and control engineer in

18        the manned space program, to an engineer tasked with developing and operating a large

19        percentage of the nation’s fuel ethanol production industry, to providing engineering design

20        and construction services in the commercial nuclear power sector, to serving as a state air

21        quality regulator in both New Mexico and Minnesota, to recently serving 8 years at the

22        New Mexico State Energy Office (Energy Minerals and Natural Resource Department,

23        Energy Conservation and Management Division), where I recently was charged with

                                                   1
                                PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                      DAREN K. ZIGICH
                                    CASE NO. 25-00079-UT

 1        implementing an Energy Conservation Code (building code) training program for building

 2        professionals throughout New Mexico.

 3

 4   Q.   Have you previously testified before this Commission?

 5   A.   Yes, to date I have provided written and oral testimony in Case No. 23-00255-UT, Case

 6        No. 23-00353-UT, Case No. 24-00089-UT, Case No. 24-00271-UT, Case No. 25-00002-

 7        UT, Case No. 25-00005-UT, Case No. 24-00266-UT, Case No. 25-00066-UT and Case No.

 8        25-00085-UT. I have also filed written testimony in Case No. 25-00035-UT and Case No.

 9        25-00048-UT.

10

11   Q.   Have you prepared any exhibits?

12   A.   Yes. Exhibits DKZ-1 and DKZ-2 are included at the end of my testimony.

13

14   Q.   What is Southwestern Public Service Company requesting in this current

15        Application?

16   A.   Southwestern Public Service Company (SPS) is requesting a rate increase based on a

17        future test year period for the 12-month period beginning December 1, 2026. SPS states it

18        will experience a revenue deficiency of $175.35 million for the Test Period, based on

19        SPS’s authorized rates approved by the Commission in Case No. 22-00286-UT (“2022

20        Rate Case”). SPS reports that the need for a revenue increase is driven largely by three

21        broad areas: “(1) significant grid investments needed to support the evolving and

22        increasing needs of customers, as well as Xcel Energy Inc. (“Xcel Energy”) and New

23        Mexico’s clean energy goals; (2) investment in a changing generation portfolio as SPS is

                                                   2

                                                DAREN K. ZIGICH

 2                 generation; and (3) the mix of SPS’s wholesale and retail customers, and the balance

 3                 between its New Mexico and Texas jurisdictions has shifted since Case No. 22-00286-

 4                 UT.”1

 3   RULE 440 REPORTING
 4   Q.      Has SPS complied with its obligation to notify the Commission in compliance with

 5           Rule 440 (17.5.440 NMAC)?

 6   A.      First, let me explain Rule 440 and how I rely on the filings in my analysis. Rule 440

 7           requires SPS to provide 30 days advance notice to the Commission for large capital

 8           projects, including transmission and distribution projects over $1 million and generation

 9           projects over $2 million (17.5.440.8 NMAC), and to update with an amended 440 Report

10           if materially significant cost overruns or scope changes occur, which they do in Rule 580

11           filings. In my role as a Staff witness, I rely on those Rule 440 filings to evaluate whether

12           projects SPS now seeks to place in rate base were planned, executed, and documented in

13           a way that is consistent with the Commission’s expectations for cost control and

14           transparency.

15

16           Assessing compliance with Rule 440, against the backdrop of a complete listing of capital

17           projects the utility wishes to rate base has not been a straight-forward process as

18           presented in SPs’s Application. Initially, the Application, including supporting testimony,

19           contained only amended 440 Reports6, with no reference to how those or the other 200

20           plus 440 reports, submitted during the Base or Linkage Period, relate to the hundreds of

11   Q.      You qualify the information as “much” of the information. What is missing from the

12           original request?

13   A.      The information provided by SPS in response to the Commission’s Bench Request is not

14           presented in a format that allows for easy comparison of the submitted 440 reports and

15           their associated cost estimate and the projects and sub-projects listed in MAK-BR-1(m).

16           As SPS witness Kietzman states:9

17                   “MAK-BR-1(m) and Rule 440 notices provide information at different levels of
18                   the Work Breakdown Structure (“WBS”). Attachment MAK-BR-1(m) reflects
19                   capital additions at WBS Level 2, which provides a more detailed view of the
20                   individual cost components of a project. By contrast, the Rule 440 notices report
21                   information at WBS Level 1, which corresponds to the overall project. Because a
22                   single WBS Level 1 project can include multiple WBS Level 2 components, the
23                   same Rule 440 notice number may appear for multiple line items in Attachment
24                   MAK-BR-1(m).”

 6   Q.         Why is that an issue?

 7   A.         Without transparency into, or knowledge of, the pre–Base Year project balances, Staff

 9              the estimates submitted in the associated 440 Report. Thus, limiting Staff’s ability to

15

16   Q.         Why is it important for Staff, the Commission and other Stakeholders to have full

17              transparency into the capital projects and costs being requested in a rate case and

18              the associated pre-project Rule 440 report filings?

19   A.         Without transparency there is no way to assess whether the projects, that meet the Rule

20              440 reporting threshold, were completed as planned and within the estimated budget.

21              Unlike projects requiring review under Section 62-9-1, NMSA 1978 or 17.9.551 NMAC,

 4   Q.   Do all these capital projects represent prudent investments?

 5   A.   Despite the difficulty in analyzing, I was able to determine that SPS’s requested capital

 6        projects are recommended by Staff to be accepted as recoverable in base rates. There is

 7        no evidence that the costs of these projects are imprudent. Based on a review of the

 8        testimony of multiple SPS witnesses, Staff believes all projects are prudent and necessary

 9        to meet reliability and resiliency goals, safety and security requirements and other

10        compliance requirements. However, Staff does highlight that SPS has provided very little

11        scope and justification information for each individual project. A comparison of SPS

12        witness Heffington’s Direct Testimony and Attachments RBH-1 through RBH-7 are more

13        difficult to review and provide less granular project specific information (including scope

14        and justification) than the same individual supplied as a PNM witness in NM PRC case

15        24-00089-UT. In that case Mr. Heffington’s Direct Testimony and Exhibit RBH-2

16        provided superior information about each project presented for inclusion in rate base.

17        While Staff understands, there is no “one way” to present the data, Staff believes the

18        information presented by PNM was easier to review and provided more information,

19        including project justification. Staff encourages the Commission to provide guidance for

20        future capital project reporting that provides for a more transparent and complete review.

13        assign costs customers in each state. Texas rejected the Cunningham BESS project and

14        therefore, SPS has limited options for cost recovery, i.e., from New Mexico ratepayers or

15        SPS’s shareholders.

21        and thus, to presumably limit SPP penalties due to SPS not meeting the SPP specified

22        Planning Reserve Margin.

13   Q.   Why is denying the SPP deficiency payment justified?

16        Unlike the PRM step increase that was the focus of the resource case 25-00066-UT, the

17        PRM SPS is apparently not going to meet due to its own imprudent planning for the

18        PRM, and is asking cost recovery for, predates the 2028-2029 winter PRM change. The

19        PRM SPS claims it will violate between now and the end of the future test year is not

20        new and thus only SPS’s management of the system is to blame and customers should not

21        pay for it. Further, given SPS now proposes charging the cost of all of the Cunningham

22        BESS, a capacity resource that limits the PRM violation, to New Mexico, New Mexico

23        customers should at a minimum receive a credit (reduction) to the SPP deficiency
